> My understanding from above is that the Bollen Stein bootstrap transform the data matrix so that simulation of the goodness-of-fit indices will be similar.

The data are transformed to be consistent with the null hypothesis--that is, so that the observed covariance matrix and mean vector are equal to their model-implied analogs.  Then the data are bootstrapped to empirically approximate the sampling distribution of the chi-squared statistic under the null hypothesis, and use it to calculate an approximate p value.  The bootstrap distribution (and the mean chi-squared) will therefore be different if your model-implied moments are substantially different from your observed sample moments.

>
> I tried again on a second dataset and that seemed fine.

When you use only R=10 bootstrap sample, there will be a LOT of sampling variability from one iteration to the next.  That's why you want to set it to ~2000 (if that's feasible for your computer).

messages.subject: Re: Multigroup invariance and second-order-factor
messages.subject_clean: Multigroup invariance and second-order-factor
messages.body_plain:
>
> a) When i use a second-order-factor in my SEM. How does "group.equal=c(...)) behave?

Second-order "loadings" are latent-variable regressions (the beta matrix, not the lambda matrix).  If those are the only latent regressions in the model, then "regressions" might work in the group.equal argument.  But you should (a) test invariance for first-order factors first, without any higher-order factors in the model, then (b) add the second-order factors after invariance is established, which will be your new "configural" model for the higher-order CFA.  In other words, follow the steps of testing invariance independently, one "level" at a time.

> Additional-Question: If it´s possible to use group.equal for second-order-factors, is the loading of the first first-order factor on the second order factor fixed to 1 or is the second order factor-mean fixed to 0 and the variance fixed to 1 for supplying a metric to the second order factor?

It's been a while since I ran a model like this, so I forget what the default behavior would be, but if you are using the"=~" operator for the second-order factors, it is probably decided by std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE/FALSE.  You'll find out when you try to fit the model.  But if I were you, I would use the lavaan() function and specify your parameters explicitly to make sure you fit the model you intend to fit.

Terry

> commonfactor4.fit<-cfa(combined.commonfactor4.model, sample.cov=combined.cov, sample.nobs=combined.n, sample.mean=combined.means, meanstructure=TRUE, group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts", "residuals", "lv.variances", "lv.covariances"), group.partial=c("PERF~~PERF", "MEM~~MEM", "PERF~~MEM"))

commonfactor4.fit@ParTable # or in matrix form using:   lavInspect(commonfactor4.fit, "partable")

Here you can see that the latent covariance "PERF~~MEM" is not constrained across groups because they do not contain the same label in the "label" column (lavaan assigns labels for simple equality constraints even if they aren't specified by the user in the syntax).

> commonfactor5.fit<-cfa(combined.commonfactor5.model, sample.cov=combined.cov, sample.nobs=combined.n, sample.mean=combined.means, meanstructure=TRUE, group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts", "residuals", "lv.variances", "lv.covariances"), group.partial=c("PERF~~PERF", "VERB~~VERB", "PERF~~VERB"))

commonfactor5.fit@ParTable

Here you can see that the latent covariance "PERF~~VERB" is mistakenly constrained across groups because the order in the parameter table is "VERB~~PERF", which is arbitrary.  You can fix this by changing the order in your "group.partial" argument.

> commonfactor6.fit<-cfa(combined.commonfactor6.model, sample.cov=combined.cov, sample.nobs=combined.n, sample.mean=combined.means, meanstructure=TRUE, group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts", "residuals", "lv.variances", "lv.covariances"), group.partial=c("MEM~~MEM", "VERB~~VERB", "MEM~~VERB"))

commonfactor6.fit@ParTable

Actually, I think the reason your model is not identified is because there is only one unique indicator of eta2 (the one with the fixed loading).  The other indicators of eta2 have cross-loadings one eta1 or eta3, so I don't think you have enough information to get a unique solution.  To check this, I tried simulating (N = 100 normal) data from your measurement model (with some arbitrary population parameters, see below), and then fitting the measurement part of your fitModel to the data.  It converged, but convergence is only a necessary (not sufficient) condition to say the model was adequately identified.  To check identification, you can then fit the same model to the model-implied covariance matrix, and you should be able to get the exact same solution (because you know the model fits perfectly to the model-implied moments).  When I fit it again, the factor loadings were all the same, but the latent (co)variances and error variances were a bit different.  When I fit the model to those model-implied moments, the estimates changed yet again.  This is a sign that the model is not actually identified, even though the estimation algorithm managed to find what appeared to be a maximum likelihood solution.

Alex

In the pv code, intercepts of the 3 factors are set to 0, while in the no-pv code, they are not constrained. Indeed. That is by design (a long story).

The way to handle this, is write a small function that 'generates'
syntax, where the value of 'V' is filled in.

Something along the lines of:

genMySyntax <- function(V = 1.0) {
     txt1 <- "F1 =~ 1*x1"
     txt2 <- paste0("x1 ~~ ", V, "*x1")
     c(txt1, txt2)
}

# small test
library(lavaan)

Data <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(100))

# reliability of x1 is assumted to be 0.80

# residual variance of x1
V <- (1-x1.rho)*var(Data$x1)

# generate syntax
myModel <- genMySyntax(V = V)

# fit model
fit <- sem(myModel, data = Data)
summary(fit)

Yves.

The only ordinal variable you appear to have nhd_walk_20min_cont, which is not an indicator or endogenous outcome of any kind in your model.  It is merely an exogenous predictor, so no assumptions about its distribution need to be made.  But unlike regression functions (e.g., lm, lme, or glm), lavaan will not automatically create dummy codes for factor variables (ordered or otherwise).  So you just have to make your own dummy codes and include those as predictors of wemwbs instead.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone,
I am a graduate student at the University of Nevada, Reno and I am working on a project to create tutorial videos for people who are familiar with SEM but new to Lavaan and/or R. The videos are currently being posted to my YouTube channel and our hope is that they will help make Lavaan as accessible as possible. Of course, the value of the videos depends on the quality of the content (e.g., free of errors, clear language), so I am posting here to invite your feedback. With the "annotate" feature on YouTube, errors can easily be corrected and clarifications can be easily inserted. I can also re-shoot a video if it is necessary.

If anyone here is interested in providing feedback, you can access the tutorial playlist at: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLFC6gleWgf9sYSqx1ROJI7IR_CRNqMxaQ

So far we have four videos dedicated to Lavaan and there are several more we have planned:

1. "R Tutorial: Installing and preparing R for Structural Equation Modeling"
2. "R Tutorial: How to Import a Dataset"
3. "R Tutorial: Path Analysis and Mediation using Lavaan"
4. "R Tutorial: Confirmatory Factor Analysis using Lavaan"

I hope that people find these videos useful and, of course, any feedback will be much appreciated!

Best regards,
Jordan

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to announce that simsem and semTools were updated in CRAN. Here are the details:

simsem, Version 0.5-11
This version is available on CRAN. Because lavaan changes the way to deal with equality constraints in parameter tables, the simsem package needs to change the codes that involves with lavaan parameter tables. This package does not have reverse compatibility. That is, the script in running simsem remains the same. However, the objects created from previous version may not run or produce erroneous results in this version.

semTools, Version 0.4-9

This version is available in CRAN. The lavaan package changes how it handles equality constraints. This version changes some functions in order to make it compatible with lavaan version 0.5-18 or higher. Furthermore, permuteMeasEq function is introduced to find the null hypothesis distribution of fit indices in measurement invariance across groups using the permutation method. Thanks to Terry Jorgensen for this contribution. spatialCorrect function is also introduced to correct standard errors in the presence of spatial autocorrelation using Moran's I. Thanks to Jarrett Byrnes for this contribution.

Links
simsem: http://simsem.org/
semTools: https://github.com/simsem/semTools/wiki

Best,
Sunthud

messages.subject_clean: "Partialling out" of predictors on endogenous DVs with predict()?
messages.body_plain:
If you want to know the effect of the DVs on the binary outcome while controlling for the IVs, then the IVs also need to be predictors of the binary outcome.  If you have the Baron & Kenny model

M ~ a*X
Y ~ b*M

then "b" is the effect of M on Y without controlling for X (thus assuming full mediation).  To control for X, you need to allow for partial mediation:

Y ~ b*M + c*X

If you want to use marginal ML and a logit link, I think that feature is available but still under development.  Check out this previous post:

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/zDcHbOnxdRg/97k6OgvFk60J

Terry

messages.subject_clean: simulateData with
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan experts,
I am doing a simple simulation and I want to replicate it (monte carlo).
In Mplus we can specify the replication by NREPS = 500 (for instance), therefore in the end I will have the averages of the estimated parameters, the standard errors, etc.

How can I do it in R?

My codes is below.

####
require(lavaan)

set.seed (12345)

# SIMULATION FOR TWO FACTOR, EACH WITH THREE INDICATORS

pop_model <-'

F1 =~ 1*X1+0.75*X2+0.64*X3
F1 ~~ 0.24*F1
F1 ~~ 0.03*F2

F2 =~ 1*X4+1.4*X5+1.3*X6
X1 ~~0.35*X1
X2 ~~0.35*X2
X3 ~~0.35*X3
X4 ~~0.35*X4
X5 ~~0.35*X5
X6 ~~0.35*X6
'

sample<-simulateData(model=pop_model, sample.nobs = 5000, model.type="sem")

####

test.model <- '
F1 =~ X1+X2+X3
F2 =~ X4+X5+X6
'

fit <- sem(test.model, data=sample, estimator="MLR")

summary(fit, standardized=TRUE)

Best,
E
